To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we used a genetically-encoded CrkII-based EGFR activity biosensor to demonstrate intratumoural heterogeneity in EGFr activity in vivo, (ii) we found macrophage-tumor cell proximity to be a major contributor to the heterogeneity, and (iii) we demonstrated that macrophages can modulate EGFR activity in tumor cells via iNOS activity.

the use of a genetically-encoded CrkII biosensor in combination with lipopolyplex-based transfection in a murine model demonstrates intratumoral heterogeneities in EGFR signalling activity, which is correlated with the proximity of tumour cells to macrophages, as well as a pharmacodynamic effect of an EGFR inhibitor.

1) liposome-based in situ transfection of a genetically encoded EGFR activity reporter in tumours is a viable approach for monitoring the pharmacodynamic effects of EGFR inhibitors; 2) the use of this approach revealed a significant degree of EGFR activity intratumoral heterogenity in a murine model for basal-like breast cancer and in human colorectal and non-small cell lung cancers; and 3) the observed intratumor heterogeneity in EGFP activity is partly accounted for
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing new technologies for the detection of EGFR signalling in tumour cells, and the application of these methods to demonstrate intratumor heterogeneity of EGRF activity in vivo.

developing novel biosensing tools for in vivo imaging and monitoring of tumour cell signalling activity, and the use of these tools to investigate the mechanisms underlying the intratumoral signalling heterogeneity.

the development of novel imaging technologies to study intracellular signalling events, particularly those related to EGFR activity, and to demonstrate their utility in monitoring therapeutic response in situ.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of FLIM-based biosensors to monitor EGFR activity in situ is an effective approach to detect intratumoral heterogeneities of EGFR activity, which can be used to monitor the pharmacodynamic response of EGFR-targeted agents.

the use of targeted lipopolyplex transfection to deliver biosensors into tumour tissue in situ, in conjunction with FLIM-based biosensing, is a useful methodology to study EGFR activity in the context of the complex tumour microenvironment.

we demonstrate that the CrkII-based fluorescent biosensor can be used to study the EGFR signalling pathway in vivo, that the Crk biosensor can detect intratumoral heterogeneities of EGFR signalling, and that the Crk II biosensor can detect EGFR activity-dependent iNOS activity and vice versa.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
FLIM-based biosensing is a powerful tool that allows for the detection of intratumoral EGFR activity heterogeneity and its regulation.
we have shown the use of lipopolyplexes as an efficient delivery system for transfecting a biosensor in vivo, and the use of this system to monitor EGFR activity in situ in a murine tumour model.
we have developed a liposome-based in-vivo transfection strategy for the detection of intratumoral signalling activity using a genetically encoded fluorescent biosensor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
intratumoral heterogeneities in EGFR activity can be detected in vivo, and that this heterogeneity can be attributed to immune microenvironment-mediated mechanisms.
the EGFR-targeted therapy may be more efficacious if the immune microenvironment is also targeted.
the immune microenvironment can have a significant effect on the activity of a receptor in cancer cells.
